name: Sauganash Hotel

placement.symbolic_location: South-east corner of Lake Street and Market Street (today Lake St and N Wacker Dr).

paint.note: Wau-Bun: 'a pretentious white two-story building, with bright-blue wooden shutters.' Painted white siding was itself remarkable at Wolf Point in 1831 — the description exists because the building stood out.

shutters.note: Wau-Bun, same sentence. The single most distinctive documented visual feature of the building.

construction.note: Balloon framing was developed in Chicago in 1832-33 and became the dominant local method. This building predates that by a year, so balloon framing is the LESS likely reading: a braced frame built onto a log core is more probable for 1831. Flagged for correction — the value is retained only until the framing question is researched, and it should probably become braced_frame. Do not treat this as settled.

cladding.note: Implied by 'white' painted finish on a frame building; clapboard is the standard cladding for the type and period. Not directly attested.

wall_height_m.note: RETAGGED 2026-08-09 from conjectural to inferred. No figure is attested for this building, but two full storeys at typical period floor heights is derivation from typology and construction practice, which is what 'inferred' means — the previous tag said 'no evidence' while this very note gave the reasoning. 5.5 m is about 18 ft: two 8 ft storeys plus floor structure and a low sill course. The DIMENSION remains uncertain; what is inferred is that it falls in this range, not that it is exactly 5.5 m.

roof_type.note: RETAGGED 2026-08-09 from conjectural to inferred, for the same reason as wall_height_m: gable is the near-universal roof form for frame buildings of this type, period and region, and both retrospective depictions show one. Typological derivation is 'inferred'. Not separately attested for this building by any period source.

gallery.note: REVISED 2026-08-09 after examining the images directly. No period source attests a gallery or porch either way, but the two surviving retrospective depictions both show the building WITHOUT one: the F. Braunhold engraving in Andreas (1884) and panel 14 of the Kurz and Allison sheet (1893) each show a plain two-story clapboard block with a modest entrance and no veranda. Caveat on independence — the Kurz and Allison panel closely follows the Andreas composition and is probably derived from it, so these are not two witnesses so much as one witness and a copy. 'No gallery' is therefore better attested than 'gallery' without being documented. See docs/RESEARCH/sauganash_hotel.md.

log_wing.note: Both retrospective depictions show a single-story LOG wing attached to the frame block at its left front, with visible log courses and corner notching under a separate shallow-pitched roof. That is almost certainly the 1829 Eagle Exchange cabin surviving as an attached wing rather than being absorbed into the frame structure — which is what the documentary sequence describes (the frame block was 'built onto' the log cabin). Same derivation caveat as the gallery: one composition, copied.

roof_pitch_deg.note: No pitch is attested. 38 degrees is mid-range for period gable framing — steep enough to shed snow, shallow enough for the timber spans available. Inferred from construction practice, not measured.

fenestration.note: No period source describes the window arrangement. A regular five-bay elevation with a centred entrance is the standard disposition for a building of this size and type, and both retrospective depictions show regular bays. The COUNT and SPACING are inference; that it was regularly fenestrated is safe.

chimneys.note: Both retrospective depictions show two. A tavern of this size needed multiple fireplaces. Not attested by a period source; the number is inference.

function.note: A tavern from 1829 and a hotel from 1831; the social centre of the settlement in the target window. Chicago's first billiard table in a public house stood here.

occupants.note: The Beaubiens owned it until 1834; the hotel chronology gives 'Davis (1835)' as operator, possibly the John Davis running the Steamboat Hotel on North Water Street. Mark Beaubien himself had moved on by the scene date — he built the Exchange Coffee House at Lake and Wells in 1834. The 1835 proprietor is a lead, not a settled fact.

"Wolf's Point and the Town of Chicago." Chicagology. Compiling A. T. Andreas, History of Chicago, and Fergus Historical Series.
"A Chronology of Early Chicago Area Hotels." Digital Research Library of Illinois History Journal.
Kinzie, Juliette A. M. Wau-Bun: The 'Early Day' in the North-West. New York: Derby & Jackson, 1856.

research_note: MILESTONE 0 REFERENCE RECORD. Two things are documented and vivid — the white two-story frame and the bright-blue shutters, both from Wau-Bun — and two things are unknown: the building's dimensions and whether it had a gallery. That combination is exactly why the per-attribute confidence model exists, and this record is deliberately the first one in the dataset. See docs/RESEARCH/sauganash_hotel.md for the source conflicts and the reasoning behind each reading. The Wigwam of 1860 stood on this site later; the hotel burned 4 March 1851.
